newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Peters avoids media, works on economic issues.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Peters avoids media, works on economic issues.

text.p: New Zealand First leader Winston Peters is doing background work on economic issues and is unlikely to attend afternoon talks with the main opposition Labour party, a spokesman said on Thursday.
Peters unexpectedly attended the fourth round of talks with the caretaker conservative National party on Thursday morning, but would not answer reporters' questions afterwards.
Peters' spokesman Mike Booker said Peters had other work to do, but had attended the morning meeting because party president Doug Woolerton was busy elsewhere.
"There is heaps of background work to do. There are other things going on than these talks," Booker said.

Asked if Peters should leave that work to researchers, Booker said: "There are things that have to be handled at that level -- at Winston's level. Economic stuff. He is the finance spokesperson -- there is a lot of work that has to be done."
He would not comment on whether the issues Peters was working on were costings of Labour's policies, as some media reports had suggested.
Asked if Peters' image had been damaged by reports on Wednesday of an alleged scuffle at the opening of a Wellington restaurant and bar, Booker said: "Not at all".
He said Peters did not want to talk to journalists after the two and a half hour meeting.
"The talks are supposed to be confidential and this issue of the Cafe Brava was run through extensively yesterday."
Leaving the meeting, caretaker Prime Minister Jim Bolger said of the talks: "They went well. They were fine." He would not comment on whether economic issues were dealt with.
Asked if Peters' unexpected absence on Wednesday and appearance on Thursday caused any problems, he said: "None whatsoever".
New Zealand First holds the balance of power after the October 12 election. It is negotiating with both Labour and National over the shape of the next government.
Bolger told Reuters the need to determine who would attend a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Manila next month did not put pressure on the coalition talks.
Asked when they would decide who to send he said: "In sufficient time. It is not a problem."
